<SUMMARY>
The Middle East conflict escalated, leading to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz since March 1, significantly impacting global oil and jet fuel markets. US President Donald Trump indicated the war is nearing completion, despite escalating strikes and high US military expenditure. Global powers are strategizing to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, with France leading efforts for international naval escorts. Concurrently, US-China technological competition intensified, with the US halting H200 AI chip production for China and China responding with calls for domestic lithography advancements and strategic plans leveraging rare earth dominance. Critical mineral supply chains are undergoing significant shifts, with Zimbabwe suspending raw lithium exports and India relaxing foreign direct investment policies for companies with minimal Chinese ownership in battery and rare earth sectors. Investments in AI infrastructure and advanced foundry technologies continued, alongside heightened cybersecurity threats linked to the Middle East conflict.
</SUMMARY>

<EWS>
The continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz presents a critical vulnerability for global energy supplies, particularly jet fuel for Europe, and risks further escalation of the Middle East conflict. The reported two-month supply of rare earth elements remaining for the US, coupled with China's dominance in processing and its strategic plan, signals an impending supply chain crunch for critical technologies. The attribution of a missile strike on an Iranian school to the US by its own military inquiry carries significant diplomatic and military ramifications. The warning from Iran that US tech firms could become military targets, and the observed cyberattacks, indicate an expanding cyber warfare front. The entry of mass-produced Russian Shahed drones into Gulf air defenses, supported by Moscow's targeting strategies, poses a growing threat to regional security.
</EWS>

<EXEC>
**Asia:** Apple has equipped its M5 MacBook Air family with the same silicon as the M5 MacBook Pro, indicating consistency in advanced silicon deployment. BYD sold 4.6 million new energy vehicles last year and operates in over 100 countries, building its own batteries, motors, semiconductors, and power electronics. HyperLight Corporation, United Microelectronics Corporation (UMC), and Wavetek Microelectronics Corporation announced a strategic partnership for high-volume foundry production of the TFLN Chiplet™ platform. Nvidia Corp. halted production of its H200 AI chips for China, aligning with US export regulations. China's semiconductor industry leaders collectively called for the development of indigenous core technologies, specifically advocating to "build China ASML." Taiwan maintains an unrivaled supply chain position for AI semiconductors. China's dual-use export regulations have shifted from indiscriminate to "Japan-targeted."

**Europe:** Nvidia Corp. plans to invest $2 billion in Nebius Group NV, a Dutch cloud provider specializing in artificial intelligence workloads, to expand data center infrastructure.

**Americas:** Nvidia Corp. launched its Nemotron Super 3 model for agentic systems, offering five-times higher throughput, and announced NemoClaw, an open-source AI agent platform for enterprise deployment with built-in security and privacy controls. Enterprises face a convergence crisis requiring new architectural blueprints for AI adoption due to fractured infrastructure across edge, cloud, and on-premises sites. An NDP private member's bill to end exemptions from Canada's export-control regime for weapons and ammunition destined for the US failed to pass. The US is reportedly considering new AI chip export regulations that would require investment as a prerequisite for purchasing chips.

**Oceania:** Australian biotech company Cortical Labs partnered with data center firm DayOne to establish two new data centers using its CL1 biological computers, aiming to address the AI energy crisis.
</EXEC>

<LITHO>
**Asia:** China's semiconductor industry leaders collectively published a statement advocating for the development of core technologies, specifically aiming to "build China ASML" to counter foreign lithography dominance. HyperLight Corporation, United Microelectronics Corporation (UMC), and Wavetek Microelectronics Corporation announced a strategic partnership for high-volume foundry production of the TFLN Chiplet™ platform.

**Europe:** Samsung is set to deploy high NA EUV machines at its 2-nanometer foundry lines. AMD displayed its first wafer with 2-nanometer chips from TSMC. Rapidus presented its first 2-nanometer wafer. Pragmatic opened the UK's first 300-nanometer semiconductor wafer manufacturing facility. Reports suggest that ASML investors should not be concerned about competition from China.
</LITHO>

<REE>
**Africa:** Liontown posted a sharp increase in production and revenue for the half-year, completing its transition to underground mining. Lynas shares have increased by 192%. Lithium Argentina AG announced an updated mineral resource and reserve estimate on the Cauchari-Olaroz brine operation, supporting a Stage 2 Development Plan. Venezuela advanced a reform that revokes state control over mining activities. Zimbabwe has suspended exports of lithium concentrates and raw minerals. An agreement was signed to develop an R1.8 billion rare earth and critical battery elements refining facility in Africa. Africa is identified as a key source of critical minerals for the global energy transition.

**Americas:** First Atlantic Nickel Corp. closed a $1.3 million non-brokered private placement to fund drilling, exploration, and metallurgical work at its Pipestone XL Atlantic Canada Nickel-Cobalt Alloy (Awaruite) Project. Brazil's rare earth reserves are estimated to be equivalent to almost twice its national GDP.

**Asia:** Beijing maintains dominance in rare earth processing, leading other nations to scramble to close the gap. A 141-page plan from China outlines how it could leverage AI and rare earths to exert pressure on the US military. The US reportedly has only two months of rare earth supplies left. China's export ban on an unspecified item, a critical raw material, has caused its price to increase 140 times, with Vietnam identified as a major world producer of 3.5 million tons.

**Oceania:** Antimony is identified as a strategic raw material with associated supply chain risks.
</REE>

<GEO>
**Asia:** Oil markets experienced heightened volatility due to the escalating Middle East conflict, with prices trending north. The International Energy Agency (IEA) agreed to release a record 400 million barrels of oil, and the US tapped 172 million barrels from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve. China has been stockpiling crude volumes in storage and diversifying oil and gas sources for months, softening its exposure to Middle Eastern energy deliveries. The Energy Drink Market in China is projected to reach USD 15.3 billion by 2032. BYD is positioned to become Formula 1’s first Chinese team by 2027. Research on microgravity-activated van der Waals InSe ferroelectric semiconductors was conducted using crystals grown on the China space station. Russia has emerged as the biggest winner in the Middle East war.

**Europe:** The closure of the Strait of Hormuz since March 1 has triggered unprecedented distortions in global jet fuel markets, pushing European aviation fuel prices to historic extremes and exposing the continent’s structural dependence on Middle Eastern supply. Central banks are scrambling as the war drives up inflation expectations, propagating through bond markets and fiscal balances.

**Americas:** South Bow Corp, a spin-off from TC Energy in 2024, is seeking to revive an oil pipeline crossing the Canada-US border.

**Oceania:** At least 85 countries have reported petrol price rises since the attacks on Iran by the US and Israel on February 28. "Armageddon" is a term used to describe Australia's current situation. The testing of AI in warfare in Iran necessitates "much more" careful thinking by New Zealand.
</GEO>

<MILITARY>
**Americas:** Powerus, a new drone maker partly owned by President Donald Trump’s two oldest sons, is competing for Pentagon contracts to supply attack drones, being flush with cash and acquiring rivals.

**Oceania:** A suspected pro-Iran hacker group has been tied to a cyberattack on Stryker. Japan is turning to dual-use technology to power a new defense industrial strategy. Female aviators are receiving modern pilot training from the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF). EOS is addressing ASX concerns regarding a high-energy laser contract with Goldrone.
</MILITARY>

<CONCLUSION>
The Middle East conflict, including the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, continues to be a primary driver of global energy market instability, with US President Donald Trump indicating a nearing conclusion to the war. The IEA and US have initiated record oil releases to mitigate price impacts. The US-China tech rivalry intensifies across AI chips and critical minerals, prompting calls for domestic innovation in China and strategic shifts in export policies from both sides. Investments are flowing into AI infrastructure and advanced semiconductor manufacturing, while the security landscape is marked by escalating military actions in West Asia and emerging cyber threats. Critical mineral supply chains, particularly for lithium and rare earths, are undergoing significant geopolitical reconfigurations as nations seek to secure resources and control processing.
</CONCLUSION>

<INDIA>
India has relaxed its foreign direct investment (FDI) regulations, specifically amending the PN3 policy to facilitate easier entry for companies from the US, Taiwan, South Korea, and Europe that have minimal Chinese ownership. This strategic shift will allow proposals for investments in advanced battery components, rare earth permanent magnets, and rare earth processing sectors to receive faster approvals. India plans to release a product list detailing which items will qualify for these expedited PN3 FDI approvals.
</INDIA>

<WEST_ASIA>
The Middle East conflict continues to escalate, with US President Donald Trump signaling that the war is nearly complete. Russia has emerged as the biggest winner in this conflict. The Strait of Hormuz has been closed since March 1, triggering unprecedented distortions in global jet fuel markets, and the escalating crisis raises the specter of prolonged closure. Global powers, led by French President Emmanuel Macron, are strategizing to reopen the vital Strait for oil and gas shipments, proposing international naval escorts.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) agreed to release a record 400 million barrels of oil, and the US tapped 172 million barrels from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve in response to the Iran war-caused supply crunch. At least 85 countries have reported petrol price rises since the US and Israel's attacks on Iran on February 28.

The US and Israel are actively pummeling Iranian military targets, and in retaliation, Iranians are striking targets across the Middle East, including a British military target. A US military inquiry determined that a missile strike on the Shajarah Tayyebeh elementary school in Iran was attributable to the United States. Iran has warned that American tech giants, including Microsoft, Palantir, and Google, could become potential targets of military action, extending the conflict into digital infrastructure. A suspected pro-Iran hacker group has been linked to a cyberattack on Stryker.

Strikes between Israel and Hezbollah have ramped up, with the Israel Defense Forces initiating a "large-scale wave of strikes on Hezbollah infrastructure" in Beirut, leading to an evacuation notice for the city. Airstrikes have pummeled both Beirut and Tehran, and drones targeted checkpoints in Tehran. US expenditure in the conflict has surpassed $11.3 billion in just six days. Iranian Shahed drones, mass-produced by Russia, are successfully penetrating Gulf air defenses, and Moscow is reportedly sharing drone targeting strategies. Iran’s authorities have warned against protests, stating that protesters acting at the behest of the US and Israel will be treated as enemies.

The US Navy denied successfully escorting an oil tanker through the Strait of Hormuz, contradicting a deleted tweet from the Energy Secretary, which Iran subsequently mocked. Iraq has called for protecting maritime corridors and energy supply routes. Reports suggest President Trump miscalculated Iran’s retaliation, leading to soaring war costs. The Gulf States are identified as a potential source of economic pressure in the energy market.
</WEST_ASIA>

<FINAL_CONCLUSION>
The confluence of an escalating Middle East conflict, intensified US-China technological competition, and evolving critical mineral supply chain dynamics will remain central to geopolitical intelligence concerns. The protracted closure of the Strait of Hormuz poses an enduring threat to global energy stability, necessitating sustained diplomatic and military efforts to de-escalate regional tensions and secure vital trade routes. Simultaneously, the global race for AI supremacy and control over strategic resources will drive continued state intervention in export controls, domestic industrial policy, and international investment frameworks. The potential for cyber warfare and the weaponization of economic dependencies, particularly in critical minerals, will define the competitive landscape in the coming period.
</FINAL_CONCLUSION>
